note: How `skynet setup --robot <model>` turns a model name into a driver library, and how far each driver has been tested. Two fields say what an installed robot needs (DRY-COVERAGE-PLAN.md F185, 12.B): transport is how the driver reaches its robot — ip (TCP, UDP, DDS, HTTP), can (SocketCAN) or raw (raw Ethernet frames, EtherCAT), or empty when it needs no network device (a serial bus, a simulated body in the same process) — because skynetk.service runs in a private network namespace that install.sh opens for exactly those and no more; python, on a driver of kind python, is the module drivers/python-host serves, the package directories (relative to drivers/) that install.sh puts on the robot, and the Python distributions the robot must already have. Kinds: prebuilt (builds with make alone; the wizard uses it built, or says how to build it), sdk (links a vendor SDK named in sdk; used built, or refused with the variable), cargo (a Rust driver in the workspace; found in the checkout's target/release, or refused with the cargo command for crate), sim (simulation-only; refused with the reason), python (runs under drivers/python-host; refused with the pointer), host (python-host itself: not a robot), library (shared code other drivers link: not a robot; linked_by names the models that are, and the refusal points at them), unmapped (no install mapping yet; refused with the README). Shipped in release bundles so the refusals work without a checkout. lib is always the Linux name: a library built on Windows or macOS will not run on the robot. Release stages (DRY-COVERAGE-PLAN.md Decisions 19): every driver that commands a physical robot carries a stage — alpha (never run on a physical robot; dry-tested only against counterparts written in this repository), beta (never run on a physical robot; dry-tested against software this repository did not write that speaks the robot's own interface — the maker's controller software, the maker's simulator, or an independent implementation of the protocol — which substrate names as the command the nightly substrate workflow runs) or stable (has run on a physical robot; no driver has, and tools/check-release-stages.mjs refuses the word until one does). tested_against says what the stage rests on. A driver that hosts other vendors' code per body (ros2_control) carries bodies instead, each with its own stage. hardware false marks a body that drives no hardware by design (mock, pendant), which carries no stage.

moteus.note: mjbots moteus servo controllers (one joint per controller) over CAN-FD on one bus, joint-level; runs under drivers/python-host
moteus.tested_against: simulated mjbots moteus controllers written in this repository, first on an in-process bus and then on a kernel virtual CAN-FD bus against controllers in another process: the register protocol, the controller's own travel read over its diagnostic channel, the hold that brings an axis up (read back, never assumed), motion in position, velocity and torque with mixed per-joint modes, the stop in the mode the operator names (zero velocity, brake or stopped), the release that is honest only where the firmware leaves the driver on, and the refusal of a controller in a fault, in a timeout, stopped or in another master's mode, or that does not answer. The registers, modes, fault codes, scales, frames and identifier are held to mjbots's own Python client (run) and firmware headers at a pinned commit by a layout check (182 checks); the link-chaos contract runs the bridge and the controllers across a CAN-FD relay (40 checks); and the maker's mode and fault registers are injected through the bridge (264 checks over 66 injected codes). Not run: a moteus, any motor behind one, or the maker's firmware

rainbow.note: a Rainbow Robotics RB arm (the RB3, RB5, RB10 and RB16 series) over the control box's two TCP ports: the command port (5000), a text protocol of script lines that the box acknowledges and then talks over with `info`, `warn` and `error` lines, and the data port (5001), where a `reqdata` is answered with one 580-byte state packet; joint-level, one `move_servo_j` per position command; runs under drivers/python-host
rainbow.tested_against: Rainbow Robotics' own client for its control boxes, `RainbowRobotics/rbpodo` at a pinned commit (Apache-2.0, fetched by SHA-256, built and run unmodified, with numpy installed by hash), against a simulated control box written in this repository: the driver's text and its reading of the 580-byte packet are held to the maker's client (103 checks: the packet's layout from a probe packet, random packets in both directions, every command byte for byte as the client writes it, the client's own typing of every kind of line the simulator says, the maker's table of 606 messages, and the client and the driver each reading what the other wrote on the same simulated control box). The driver's refusals, bring-up, state, commands, stop, motions and session run against the simulated control box on loopback ports (741 checks); the sim half of SCTS passes through the real ABI (37 passed, 0 failed); the link-chaos contract runs both connections through a relay that delays, stalls and blackholes them (30 checks); and the maker's own table of 606 message codes (as errors and as warnings) and the packet document's device error, software stop, collision, joint-word, SOS-state and mode fields are injected (5,340 checks over 1,335 codes). The bridge was also run once, by hand, against the maker's Virtual Control Box (RBVirtualSimulator 8.4.4 in QEMU: 12 checks, with its arm unpowered), which nothing in a workflow runs. The comparison pins two places the maker's client falls short (F321, F322: it writes six significant digits where the driver writes six decimals, and it reads a multi-line message as one line and the rest unknown) and the run against the Virtual Control Box three where the box differs from the maker's document or from a controller (F319 to F320, F323: a `time` that is not a float second, a `task stop` that does not latch and a `task pause` that is not a stop, and a box that boots with no arm power so that `move_j` goes nowhere). Not run: a Rainbow arm, a Rainbow control box or its firmware; the simulated control box is accepted by the client because it was made to be (F15)

tello.note: a Ryze (DJI) Tello or Tello EDU quadcopter over the SDK 2.0 User Guide's UDP text commands: commands on port 8889, answered `ok`, `error` or a value, and the state string the drone pushes to port 8890; an aerial body with no joints, command-level (motions in metres, degrees and percent under vendor.tello.task, the pose is the height); runs under drivers/python-host
tello.tested_against: a simulated Tello written in this repository, on loopback UDP ports: the guide's commands, replies and 10 Hz state string, a motion answered `ok` when it is done, a battery that drains and the drone's own 15-second watchdog. The driver's text and state string are held to djitellopy 2.5.0 (MIT), the client of the same guide that everyone else uses, installed by hash and run unmodified (55 checks: every command byte for byte as djitellopy writes it, sixty random state strings read by both, what each takes a reply for, and djitellopy and the driver each moving or reading the same simulated drone); djitellopy is another person's reading of the guide, not the maker's software. The driver's refusals, handshake, state, motions, stop, keepalive and lines run against the simulated drone (441 checks); the sim half of SCTS passes through the real ABI (34 passed, 0 failed); and the link-chaos contract runs the command and state flows through relays that delay, stall, lose, repeat, reorder, truncate and corrupt datagrams (68 checks). The comparison pins where djitellopy and the driver differ on purpose (F324, F325: it resends a motion whose reply was lost, and takes any reply with `ok` inside it for success). Not run: a Tello or a Tello EDU, the maker's firmware or app, or any real radio: the maker publishes no simulator, its sample client is on an address that no longer answers, and the guide has no table of error codes
